newsitem.title: USA: Aflatoxin found in Texas grain sorghum.
newsitem.headline: Aflatoxin found in Texas grain sorghum.

text.p: Texas officials said Thursday they had found the carcinogen aflatoxin in samples of grain sorghum.
Texas state chemist George Latimer said the toxin, which is produced by a fungus, was discovered in tests of grains from 11 counties and at levels exceeding federal guidelines.

"We're finding that the sorghum crop has a fair amount of aflatoxin, enough that people can't blindly substitute sorghum for corn," he said in a statement. "Everyone should be testing sorghum as well as cottonseed and corn."
He said much of the sorghum was found to have 70 to 80 parts per billion of aflatoxin, but one sample had 400 ppb.
According to U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidelines, the maximum permissible level for aflatoxin contamination is 20 ppb in food for humans and feed for some animals.
Officials say a severe drought that struck the state earlier this summer contributed to the outbreak of aflatoxin, which was found earlier in Texas corn crops.
